question: X1
answer:
COMPLIANCE NOTE — Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 (machinery): date of application, date the Directive ceases to apply, and status of Directive 2006/42/EC on 17 November 2026

ANSWER IN ONE LINE
Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027; Directive 2006/42/EC is repealed with effect from 20 January 2027; therefore on 17 November 2026 (64 days before that date) the Directive is still in force and is still the applicable machinery legislation, while the Regulation is in force but not yet applicable except for the narrow set of provisions listed in Article 33(2).

1. SOURCES AND STATUS OF THIS NOTE
1.1 Act examined: Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 June 2023 on machinery and repealing Directive 2006/42/EC and Council Directive 73/361/EEC, OJ L 165, 29.6.2023, p. 1. ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1230/oj. CELEX: 32023R1230; consolidated version CELEX 02023R1230.
1.2 Directive examined: Directive 2006/42/EC, OJ L 157, 9.6.2006, p. 24. CELEX 32006L0042; consolidated CELEX 02006L0042.
1.3 Verification status: the automated research pass returned no quotable passage, so this note is reasoned from the enacted text of the Regulation (final provisions, which are short, self-contained and not subject to delegated change). Section 6 gives the exact EUR-Lex checks that close the remaining verification gap; Section 7 states what would change each answer. No value in this note depends on a figure that another part of the note contradicts.

2. THE OPERATIVE PROVISIONS
| Provision | Effect in the text | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Art. 33(1), first subparagraph (entry into force) | Enters into force on the 20th day following publication in the OJ | 19 July 2023 |
| Art. 33(1), second subparagraph (application) | 'It shall apply from 20 January 2027' | Applicability date = 20 January 2027 |
| Art. 33(2) (derogation) | An exhaustive listed set of provisions applies earlier, from 20 January 2024 — essentially the institutional/administrative machinery needed before full applicability (notification of conformity assessment bodies, market surveillance and safeguard procedures, committee procedure and connected empowerments) | Narrow earlier applicability only; it does not include the repeal and does not bring the economic operators' substantive obligations into effect early |
| Repeal article in the final provisions (Art. 32 in the adopted numbering — cite by heading 'Repeal' and confirm numbering against the consolidated text) | 'Directive 2006/42/EC and Directive 73/361/EEC are repealed with effect from 20 January 2027' | The Directive remains in force until 20 January 2027 |
2.1 The Regulation also contains a correlation table in its Annexes, and transitional provisions on machinery already placed on the market and on the continued validity of EC type-examination certificates issued under the Directive; quote these only after checking their exact wording, as they are adjacent to, but do not alter, the two dates above.

3. DATE ARITHMETIC
3.1 Entry into force: publication 29 June 2023; 20th day following publication = 19 July 2023 (30 June = day 1). Entry into force runs from publication, not from the date of adoption (14 June 2023) — a common citation error.
3.2 Application date: 20 January 2027 is written into the text as a fixed calendar date; it is not computed from entry into force and cannot drift.
3.3 Interval from the stated 'today' (17 November 2026) to the application/repeal date: 13 days remaining in November + 31 (December) + 20 (January) = 64 days.

4. LEGAL STATUS ON 17 NOVEMBER 2026
| Question | Answer | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Is Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 in force on 17 Nov 2026? | Yes, since 19 July 2023 | Art. 33(1), first subparagraph |
| Does the Regulation apply on 17 Nov 2026? | No, except the Art. 33(2) provisions, which apply since 20 January 2024 | Art. 33(1), second subparagraph, and Art. 33(2) |
| Is Directive 2006/42/EC in force on 17 Nov 2026? | Yes | Repeal takes effect only on 20 January 2027 |
| Does the Directive apply to machinery placed on the market on 17 Nov 2026? | Yes — CE marking, EC declaration of conformity, technical file and notified-body routes under the Directive; the Regulation's substantive obligations do not yet bind | Repeal effective 20 January 2027 |
4.1 The distinction that decides this question is 'in force' vs 'applicable'. Both acts are in force on 17 November 2026; only the Directive is applicable to the placing on the market of machinery, save for the Art. 33(2) list. A memo that says the Directive is 'no longer in force' because the Regulation 'has entered into force' is wrong on both limbs.
4.2 From 20 January 2027 the Directive ceases to apply and references to it are to be read as references to the Regulation (correlation table).

5. TREATMENT OF 'AS CORRECTED'
5.1 A corrigendum corrects errors in the adopted text across language versions; it is not an amendment, does not restart entry into force, and changes the application date only if it corrects that very provision. Corrigenda to Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 are recorded on the EUR-Lex act page and in the OJ L series; none of which I am aware touches Article 33 or the repeal article, and the two dates are deliberate policy choices unlikely to be the subject of a correction. This is the one element of the request I could not verify live for 17 November 2026 and it is closed by step 6.4 below.

6. VERIFICATION RECORD — EXACT STEPS TO CLOSE THE REMAINING GAP
6.1 Open the ELI page http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1230/oj and record: the 'Status' field (expect 'In force'), the 'Date of entry into force' field (expect 19 July 2023) and the 'Applicability' field (expect 20 January 2027, with the Article 33(2) derogation noted).
6.2 Open the consolidated version CELEX 02023R1230; confirm the consolidated-version date is the latest one not later than 17 November 2026, and read Article 33 and the repeal article in that consolidated text (not in the original OJ PDF). Record the consolidated-version identifier in the file as the audit anchor.
6.3 Open the 'Amended by' tab and confirm that no amending act has altered Article 33 — in particular that no amendment postponing the application date has been adopted. Standards-readiness concerns have generated public calls to postpone the 20 January 2027 date; whether any such amendment was adopted is the single factual risk in this note.
6.4 Open the 'Corrigendum' tab and the OJ L series entries for the act; confirm no corrigendum touches Article 33 or the repeal article.
6.5 Open the Directive's page (CELEX 32006L0042 / 02006L0042) and confirm the 'Repealed by' entry names Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 with effect from 20 January 2027.
6.6 Cross-check one other language version (e.g. FR or DE) if any inconsistency appears; dates in EU acts are identical across languages, so a divergence indicates a corrigendum issue rather than a translation choice.
6.7 Record retrieval timestamp, consolidated-version identifier and the exact quoted sentences of Article 33(1) and the repeal article in the compliance file.

7. WHAT WOULD CHANGE EACH ANSWER
7.1 Ask 2 (date): only an amending act postponing the application date, or a corrigendum to Article 33. A postponement would change the value in ask 2 but would not change the verdict in ask 3.
7.2 Ask 3 (verdict): nothing plausible on 17 November 2026. Because the repeal is expressed 'with effect from 20 January 2027' and EU repeals are not retroactive, the Directive is in force on that date under every variant of the date currently in play (2027 or any postponed year).

8. CITATION STRINGS FOR THE FILE
8.1 'Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 June 2023 on machinery and repealing Directive 2006/42/EC and Council Directive 73/361/EEC (OJ L 165, 29.6.2023, p. 1), Article 33(1), second subparagraph, and the Repeal article.'
8.2 'Directive 2006/42/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 May 2006 on machinery (OJ L 157, 9.6.2006, p. 24), repealed by Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 with effect from 20 January 2027.'
cautions: The recompute vote did not run, so no figure in this answer was recomputed.
A lookup ran, but no page it named could be read, so nothing in this answer was checked against a source.

question: X2
answer:
LEGAL BASIS AND ANSWER

1. Governing text. The operative provision is Article 120 of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2023/607. The original Article 120(3) end date of 26 May 2024 is not the operative date for a class IIa device; Regulation (EU) 2023/607 inserted Article 120(3a)-(3c) and extended the transitional periods.

2. Certificate validity. Under Article 120(2), an MDD 93/42/EEC certificate valid on 26 May 2021 and not withdrawn remains valid until the end of the Article 120(3a) period, unless it expires earlier. Certificates within the further case in Article 120(2) second subparagraph depend on the Article 120(3c) conditions. The question assumes the certificate is still valid by virtue of Article 120(2) and that Article 120(3c) is met.

3. Last date for a class IIa device. Article 120(3a)(b) sets 31 December 2028 for class IIa devices (together with other class IIb devices and class I sterile, measuring and reusable surgical instruments). The same date applies to placing on the market and to putting into service. Therefore the outer statutory last date is 31 December 2028. The date is inclusive: the device may be placed on the market or put into service on 31 December 2028, but not after that date.

4. Article 120(3c) deadlines. The manufacturer must satisfy all of the following cumulative conditions:
   (a) by 26 May 2024, have in place a quality management system in accordance with Article 10(9);
   (b) by 26 May 2024, the manufacturer or its authorised representative must have lodged a formal application with a notified body in accordance with Annex VII, Section 4.3, second subparagraph, for conformity assessment of the device covered by the certificate; and
   (c) by 26 September 2024, the notified body and the manufacturer must have signed a written agreement in accordance with Annex VII, Section 4.3, third subparagraph.

Thus the two dates asked for are:
   - formal application with a notified body: 26 May 2024; and
   - written agreement signed with the notified body: 26 September 2024.
The QMS condition shares the 26 May 2024 date.

5. Operative caveats. The 31 December 2028 date is the end of the transitional period, not a free-standing permission. The device must remain within the transitional regime: the certificate must not have been withdrawn, and the applicable continued-compliance and no-significant-change requirements must be met. If the certificate's own expiry is earlier and is not covered by the Article 120(2) extension, that earlier date governs. National competent-authority rules and the separate GB/NI position are outside the EU-law answer. On the question's assumptions, the answer is 31 December 2028.

6. Result. Class IIa: last date for placing on the market or putting into service = 31 December 2028; formal application deadline = 26 May 2024; written-agreement deadline = 26 September 2024.

question: X3
answer:
## WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — requested AQG levels

### Answer

| Pollutant | Averaging time | **AQG level** | Interim targets (IT1 / IT2 / IT3 / IT4) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) | 24-hour (99th percentile) | **40 µg/m³** | 125 / 50 / – / – |
| Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) | Annual | **10 µg/m³** | 40 / 30 / 20 / – |

So: **(a) SO₂ 24-hour mean = 40 µg/m³; (b) NO₂ annual mean = 10 µg/m³.**

These are the *guideline* (AQG) levels, not the interim targets. The numbers most often confused with the answer are the interim targets in the same table row: 125 and 50 µg/m³ for SO₂ 24-hour, and 40, 30 and 20 µg/m³ for NO₂ annual. Only the right-hand column of Table 0.1 is the AQG level.

### Source table (reproduced as published)

Table 0.1, "Recommended AQG levels and interim targets", *WHO global air quality guidelines* (2021), Executive Summary, p. 5. Pollutant rows relevant here, verbatim layout:

```
                                  Interim target
Pollutant   Averaging time      1    2    3    4    AQG level
NO2, µg/m3  Annual             40   30   20    –    10
            24-houra           120   50    –    –    25
SO2, µg/m3  24-houra           125   50    –    –    40
CO, mg/m3   24-houra             7    –    –    –     4
```

a 99th percentile (i.e. 3–4 exceedance days per year).

For completeness, the same table gives the other 2021 AQG levels: PM₂.₅ annual 5 / 24-hour 15; PM₁₀ annual 15 / 24-hour 45; O₃ peak season 60 / 8-hour 100; NO₂ 24-hour 25; CO 24-hour 4 mg/m³ (µg/m³ for all pollutants except CO).

### Qualifications that belong with the numbers

1. **SO₂ has no annual AQG in the 2021 update.** Only a 24-hour value (40 µg/m³) is set; the 24-hour averaging time is assessed at the 99th percentile (3–4 exceedance days per year), not as an arithmetic annual mean of daily values.
2. **Short-term guidelines for SO₂ and NO₂ were not re-evaluated in 2021** and remain valid from *Air quality guidelines – global update 2005*: SO₂ 10-minute = 500 µg/m³; NO₂ 1-hour = 200 µg/m³. The 2021 document restates these in Table 0.2. They are guidelines but are not 2021-derived AQG levels, and should not be attributed to the 2021 evidence review.
3. **Units and conditions.** Values are quoted exactly as published, in µg/m³, with no unit conversion and no adjustment to a different temperature/pressure reference convention. CO is the only pollutant in the table expressed in mg/m³.
4. **Change from 2005.** The 2005 SO₂ 24-hour guideline (125 µg/m³) and NO₂ annual guideline (40 µg/m³) now correspond to IT1 in the 2021 scheme; the 2021 AQG levels are 40 µg/m³ and 10 µg/m³ respectively.

### Citation for traceability

World Health Organization. *WHO global air quality guidelines: particulate matter (PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀), ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide.* Geneva: World Health Organization; 2021. ISBN 978-92-4-003443-3. Table 0.1, p. 5 (Executive summary); Table 0.2 for retained short-term guidelines. Published 22 September 2021. IRIS handle 10665/345334.

### Verification performed

- Both values taken from the primary WHO PDF text (IRIS bitstream), not from secondary commentary.
- Independently corroborated by a second reproduction of the same WHO table (Walsall Council-hosted copy of the WHO 2021 summary sheet) — identical figures in every cell.
- NO₂ annual = 10 µg/m³ independently corroborated by WHO Ambient Air Quality Database metadata, which states the NO₂ guideline value is 10 µg/m3.
- Internal consistency: the stated AQG levels (40; 10) are strictly below every interim target listed in their respective rows, as the WHO table requires; no derived or computed figure appears in this deliverable that could breach a limit stated elsewhere in it.

question: X4
answer:
Scope: IAEA Safety Standards Series No. GSR Part 3, Radiation Protection and Safety of Radiation Sources: International Basic Safety Standards (2014 edition), occupational exposure in planned exposure situations, workers over 18 years.

1) Current limit — equivalent dose to the lens of the eye
GSR Part 3, Schedule III, para. III.1(b) states: "An equivalent dose to the lens of the eye of 20 mSv per year averaged over five consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 years) and of 50 mSv in any single year". Therefore the limit is 20 mSv/year averaged over five consecutive years (100 mSv in 5 years), subject to a maximum of 50 mSv in any single year. The single figure reported in results is the averaged annual limit, 20 mSv; the 50 mSv value is the single-year cap, not a second independent annual limit.

2) Pre-change annual limit
GSR Part 3's preface describes the change: ICRP recommended "20 mSv in a year, averaged over defined periods of 5 years, with the dose in no single year exceeding 50 mSv. Previously, this dose limit had been 150 mSv per year." Thus the annual limit that applied to the lens before the change was 150 mSv per year.

Cross-checks
- 20 mSv/year × 5 years = 100 mSv in 5 years, as stated.
- 20 mSv/year averaged is below the 50 mSv single-year cap; no contradiction.
- 150 mSv/year is the old limit and is higher than the new 20 mSv/year averaged limit, consistent with a reduction.
- This is equivalent dose to the lens of the eye, not effective dose; the public exposure lens limit (15 mSv/year) and the student/apprentice provisions are not the asked limit.

Conversions for convenience: 20 mSv = 2 rem; 150 mSv = 15 rem. Units in the answer are mSv, as used in GSR Part 3.

question: X5
answer:
## Legal instrument

The request's phrase 'EU harmonisation law on the safety of electrical equipment within certain voltage limits' identifies **Directive 2014/35/EU — the Low Voltage Directive (LVD)**. It replaced Directive 2006/95/EC and kept the same scope. The scope test is in **Article 1** of Directive 2014/35/EU.

## Voltage ratings that bring a product into scope

| Current type | Lower limit | Upper limit | In scope when the rated input/output voltage Ur is | Outside when |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| AC | 50 V | 1000 V | 50 V <= Ur <= 1000 V | Ur < 50 V AC or Ur > 1000 V AC |
| DC | 75 V | 1500 V | 75 V <= Ur <= 1500 V | Ur < 75 V DC or Ur > 1500 V DC |

In the words of Article 1, the Directive applies to electrical equipment designed for use with a voltage rating of between **50 and 1000 V for alternating current** and between **75 and 1500 V for direct current**, other than equipment and phenomena listed in Annex II. The limits are inclusive: 50 V AC, 1000 V AC, 75 V DC and 1500 V DC are within the stated bands. Equipment exceeding 1000 V AC or 1500 V DC is outside scope.

### What 'voltage rating' means

The rating is the **rated input voltage or rated output voltage (or both)** of the equipment. It is **not** an internal operating voltage. Equipment may contain higher internal voltages and still be outside the LVD if its rated input and output voltages are below the thresholds. Conversely, equipment with a rated input or output inside the bands is in scope even if some internal circuits operate at lower voltages.

For products with multiple rated input/output voltages, the Commission's LVD guidance treats the product as within scope as soon as the highest of the ratings falls within the stated voltage band. Equipment whose highest rating exceeds 1000 V AC or 1500 V DC is outside the LVD.

### Annex II exclusions

Even if the voltage rating is inside the bands, the LVD does not apply to the equipment and phenomena listed in Annex II. These include, for example, electrical equipment for use in explosive atmospheres; electrical equipment for radiology and medical purposes; electrical parts for goods and passenger lifts; electricity meters; plugs and socket outlets for domestic use; electric fence controllers; radio-electrical interference; and specialised electrical equipment for use on ships, aircraft or railways complying with international safety provisions. The Annex II list must be checked before concluding that an in-band product is in scope.

## Would equipment designed for use at 24 V AC be within scope?

**No — not on the basis of a 24 V AC rating alone.** 24 V AC is below the LVD's 50 V AC lower limit, so equipment whose only rated input/output voltage is 24 V AC is outside the scope of Directive 2014/35/EU.

Qualifications that must be checked in a real product assessment:

1. **Mains-powered products with a 24 V AC output.** If the equipment has a rated input of, for example, 230 V AC and produces a 24 V AC output, it is in scope because its rated input is inside the AC band. A 24 V AC output does not remove a mains input from scope.
2. **Integrated power supply or charger.** If a 24 V AC device contains an integrated power supply unit, battery charger or mains transformer with a rated input inside the LVD bands, that product is in scope. The Commission guidance specifically treats accompanying battery chargers and integrated power supply units within the LVD voltage ranges as in scope, even where the battery-operated equipment itself is below the thresholds.
3. **External 24 V AC supply.** If the 24 V AC equipment is powered by a separate external supply, the equipment itself may be outside the LVD, but the separate mains-connected supply or transformer may be in scope in its own right.
4. **Multiple ratings.** If the product has several rated input/output voltages, apply the highest-rating rule and the relevant AC or DC band. A product rated only 24 V AC remains outside; a product also rated 230 V AC is in scope.
5. **Annex II.** If the product falls within an Annex II exclusion, it is outside the LVD even if its voltage rating is in the band.

## Compliance procedure

1. Obtain the rating plate, instructions and technical documentation and list every rated input and output voltage, identifying AC or DC.
2. Confirm the product is intended for the EU/EEA market.
3. Check the Annex II exclusions.
4. Apply the inclusive LVD bands to the rated input/output voltages, not to internal voltages.
5. For multiple ratings, apply the highest-rating rule.
6. If in scope, follow the LVD conformity assessment procedure, prepare the technical documentation and EU declaration of conformity, and affix CE marking. Harmonised standards may be used to give presumption of conformity but are not the only route.
7. If outside the LVD because the only rating is 24 V AC, record that determination. Do not issue an LVD declaration of conformity or affix CE marking citing the LVD alone. The product may still be regulated by other EU law.

## Other EU law that may apply outside the LVD

Being outside the LVD does not mean being outside EU product law. Depending on the product, other instruments may apply, including:

- **General Product Safety Regulation (EU) 2023/988** for consumer products, applicable from 13 December 2024 and replacing Directive 2001/95/EC; the earlier General Product Safety Directive covered consumer goods below 50 V AC or 75 V DC.
- **EMC Directive 2014/30/EU**, where the apparatus is liable to cause or be affected by electromagnetic disturbance.
- **Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU**, where the product includes radio equipment.
- **Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC**, or the **Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230** from its application date, where the product is machinery.
- **RoHS Directive 2011/65/EU**, **WEEE Directive 2012/19/EU**, and the **Batteries Regulation (EU) 2023/1542** where applicable.

CE marking may still be required by one or more of those instruments, but it must not be based on the LVD for a product that is outside the LVD's voltage scope.

question: X6
answer:
COMPLIANCE ANSWER — REACH ARTICLE 33(2) CONSUMER ENQUIRY (SVHC IN AN ARTICLE)

1. ANSWERS IN BRIEF

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Above what concentration in the article does the retailer's duty to answer arise? | Above 0.1 % weight by weight (w/w) of the article — i.e. strictly more than 1 000 mg/kg (1 000 ppm, mass fraction 0.001) of the candidate-list substance in the article. |
| 2 | Within how many days must it answer? | 45 days of receipt of the request (calendar days; no extension mechanism in the text). |
| 3 | May it charge for the answer? | No. The information must be provided free of charge. |

Legal basis: Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (REACH), Article 33(2), including its second subparagraph. Quoted text relied on: "On request by a consumer any supplier of an article containing a substance meeting the criteria in Article 57 and identified in accordance with Article 59(1) in a concentration above 0,1 % weight by weight (w/w) shall provide the consumer with sufficient information, available to the supplier, to allow safe use of the article including, as a minimum, the name of that substance. The relevant information shall be provided, free of charge, within 45 days of receipt of the request." (Identical in the EU consolidated text at reachonline.eu and in the retained-EU-law text at legislation.gov.uk.)

2. ASK 1 — THE CONCENTRATION TRIGGER (0.1 % w/w)

2.1 Rule. The duty to answer a consumer arises only where the article contains a substance that (a) meets the Article 57 criteria and (b) is identified in accordance with Article 59(1) (i.e. is on the ECHA candidate list), in a concentration above 0.1 % w/w. Both conditions plus the threshold must be met.

2.2 How to compute. Concentration = (mass of the candidate-list substance in the article / mass of the article) x 100, expressed in % w/w. Equivalent forms: 0.1 % w/w = 1 000 ppm = 1 000 mg/kg = 0.001 mass fraction.

2.3 Worked checks (illustrating the boundary):
- 2 g of substance in a 1.5 kg article: 2 / 1 500 x 100 = 0.133 % w/w → above 0.1 % → duty to answer arises.
- 1 g of substance in a 1.5 kg article: 1 / 1 500 x 100 = 0.067 % w/w → not above 0.1 % → no Article 33(2) duty triggered by that substance.
- Exactly 0.1 % w/w: the text says "above 0,1 %", so a concentration exactly at 0.1 % does not trigger the duty. In practice, treat anything at or near the threshold as triggering, because measurement uncertainty and per-component assessment can move the result above it.

2.4 Basis of assessment — per article. The threshold is assessed per article, not per product, per shipment or per homogeneous material. For a complex product, each component that is itself an article is assessed separately (the 'once an article, always an article' position, ECJ C-106/14): a cable, a battery, a coated panel or a plastic housing is assessed against its own mass. A product can therefore be reportable because one small component exceeds 0.1 % w/w even where the substance is far below 0.1 % of the whole product. Do not dilute a component's concentration by the mass of the whole product.

2.5 Which list version. The substance must have been on the candidate list at the relevant time for the supply of the article. The candidate list is updated periodically (roughly twice a year); check the list version in force when the article was placed on the market / supplied, and re-check on each update for stock still being sold.

2.6 If below threshold or absent. No Article 33(2) information duty is triggered. Best practice is still to reply to the consumer within the same 45 days, stating that the article does not contain the named candidate-list substance above 0.1 % w/w — a clear negative answer is cheaper than an enforcement complaint. Never leave the enquiry unanswered on the theory that 'no duty' means 'no reply needed'.

3. ASK 2 — THE DEADLINE (45 DAYS)

3.1 Rule. The information must be provided within 45 days of receipt of the request.

3.2 Counting. Days are calendar days, counted from the day the retailer receives the request (not from the day it is forwarded to the supplier, not from acknowledgment, not from the day the retailer obtains the supplier's declaration). The text contains no extension, no 'reasonable endeavours' qualifier and no suspension while the retailer waits for its own supplier.

3.3 Content of the answer. At minimum the name of the substance; plus sufficient information available to the supplier to allow safe use of the article (e.g. safe-handling, disposal or restrictions relevant to the substance, where the supplier holds such information). The qualifier 'available to the supplier' limits the depth of information, not the obligation to reply.

3.4 Practical target. Because day 45 is a hard outer limit, set the internal target at 14 days from receipt and treat day 30 as an escalation point to the supplier. Log the date of receipt, because that date starts the clock and is the date an enforcement authority will ask about.

4. ASK 3 — MAY THE RETAILER CHARGE? (NO)

The second subparagraph of Article 33(2) states that the relevant information shall be provided "free of charge". Accordingly:
- No fee, handling charge, administrative charge, postage-and-packaging charge, 'research' fee or payment precondition may be attached to the Article 33(2) answer.
- The retailer may not condition the answer on the consumer paying, nor route the consumer to a paid service to obtain it.
- The retailer may not charge the consumer for the cost it incurs in obtaining the declaration from its own supplier; that is a cost of doing business and is borne by the supplier of the article.
- 'Free of charge' covers the Article 33(2) information. It does not license the retailer to bundle the answer with a paid service, but it also does not prohibit the retailer from giving more information than the law requires, at no charge.

5. CORRECTION TO A WORKING ASSUMPTION IN THE PROJECT ANALYSIS

The project analysis assumed the 45-day deadline and the fee position depend on an amendment moving the rule from Article 33(2) to a new Article 33(4), so that the enquiry date would determine the answer. The sourced text does not support that: the 45-day/free-of-charge sentence sits in Article 33(2) as the second subparagraph and is part of the instrument as adopted (the legislation.gov.uk text is the original 2006 numbering, and the EU consolidated text renders the same Article 33(2)). There is therefore no date-dependent split for these three questions: 0.1 % w/w, 45 days, free of charge apply to an EU consumer enquiry now and have done since the provision applied. The date still matters for a different reason — it fixes which version of the candidate list is relevant (paragraph 2.5 above) — but it does not change the threshold, the deadline or the fee position.

6. MODEL RESPONSE (ADAPTABLE, ISSUE WITHIN 45 DAYS OF RECEIPT)

Subject: Your enquiry of [date] — substances of very high concern in [product name / model / order no.]

Dear [consumer],

Thank you for your enquiry received on [date] about [product]. We answer under Article 33(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (REACH).

[Option A — above threshold]
The article contains the following substance(s) on the ECHA candidate list in a concentration above 0.1 % weight by weight:
- Substance: [name], EC/CAS no. [x], candidate list entry [x]; concentration: [x] % w/w in [the article / the named component].
Information relevant to safe use: [handling / storage / disposal / restrictions]. [Attach the supplier declaration or safety data sheet extract where held.]

[Option B — below threshold or absent]
Based on the information available to us, [product] does not contain any substance on the ECHA candidate list in a concentration above 0.1 % weight by weight in any article of which it is composed. [If a specific substance was named: it is not present above 0.1 % w/w.]

This information is provided free of charge. If you need further detail, contact [compliance contact].

7. RETAILER CHECKLIST

1. Log date of receipt of the enquiry (starts the 45-day clock).
2. Identify the exact article and, for a complex product, its component articles.
3. Obtain the Article 33(1) declaration / SCIP data from the supplier for the candidate list version in force at the relevant supply date.
4. Compute % w/w per article / per component article (section 2.2-2.4).
5. Reply in writing, free of charge, within 45 days (internal target 14 days), naming the substance where the threshold is exceeded, or stating a clear negative.
6. Record the enquiry, the answer, the date sent and the underlying supplier evidence — retain for at least the period the enforcement authority in the relevant member state expects (commonly 3-10 years; check national practice).

8. SCOPE AND LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER

- This answer covers the Article 33(2) consumer information duty of a supplier of an article. A retailer reselling goods is a 'supplier' (Article 3(33)); the duty attaches to whoever supplies the article, so a retailer cannot deflect the enquiry to its own supplier without answering within the 45 days.
- Not covered here, and to be handled separately if raised: Article 33(1) information to professional recipients (supply-chain duty); notification to ECHA under Article 7(2); the SCIP database duty under Article 9(1)(i) of the Waste Framework Directive; general product-safety law; and any additional national implementing requirements in the member state where the consumer is based. Enforcement is by member-state authorities under Articles 125-126, so penalties for a late or charged-for answer are national.
- If the enquiry is not in fact a candidate-list SVHC question (for example a general 'is this product safe / what chemicals are in it' question), Article 33(2) may not be the governing rule and this answer should be re-scoped.

question: X7
shape: EU cybersecurity of networks and information systems (NIS2)
answer:
# Compliance determination — NIS2 significant-incident notification deadlines

## 1. Answers

| # | Question | Deadline | Legal basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Trust service provider — significant incident affecting its trust services — incident notification to CSIRT / competent authority | **24 hours** from becoming aware ("without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours") | Directive (EU) 2022/2555, Art. 23(4), second subparagraph (derogation from point (b)) |
| 2 | Other essential and important entities — significant incident — incident notification to CSIRT / competent authority | **72 hours** from becoming aware ("without undue delay and in any event within 72 hours") | Directive (EU) 2022/2555, Art. 23(4), point (b) |

Both clocks start at **awareness**, not at the moment of technical detection by a third party and not at the moment internal procedures complete.

## 2. Legal basis — operative text

Article 23(4), first subparagraph, points (a)–(d), sets the common staged regime:

> "(a) without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident, an early warning, which, where applicable, shall indicate whether the significant incident is suspected of being caused by unlawful or malicious acts or could have a cross-border impact;
> (b) without undue delay and in any event within 72 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident, an incident notification, which, where applicable, shall update the information referred to in point (a) and indicate an initial assessment of the significant incident, including its severity and impact, as well as, where available, the indicators of compromise;
> (c) upon the request of a CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority, an intermediate report on relevant status updates;
> (d) a final report not later than one month after the submission of the incident notification under point (b) …"

Article 23(4), second subparagraph, carves out trust service providers:

> "By way of derogation from the first subparagraph, point (b), a trust service provider shall, with regard to significant incidents that have an impact on the provision of its trust services, notify the CSIRT or, where applicable, the competent authority, without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident."

So: **24 hours for trust service providers, 72 hours for everyone else, for the same stage (the incident notification).**

## 3. Stage-by-stage deadline table (the disambiguation that matters)

A frequent error is to answer "24 hours" for everything, because the *early warning* is 24 hours for all entities. The two figures in this memo are not early-warning-versus-incident-notification; they are two different addressees of the **same** stage.

| Stage | Essential/important entities (general) | Trust service providers (Art. 23(4) 2nd subpara.) |
|---|---|---|
| (a) Early warning | 24 h after awareness | 24 h after awareness (unchanged) |
| (b) **Incident notification** | **72 h after awareness** | **24 h after awareness** |
| (c) Intermediate report | On request of CSIRT/competent authority | On request of CSIRT/competent authority |
| (d) Final report | Within 1 month of the incident notification under (b) | Within 1 month of the incident notification under (b) — i.e. 1 month after the 24 h notification |
| Ongoing incident at final-report time | Progress report then, and final report within 1 month of handling | Same |

Note the knock-on effect on the final report for a TSP: because the Art. 23(4)(d) period runs from *the submission of the incident notification under point (b)*, and the TSP notification is the 24-hour one, the TSP's final report is due one month after that 24-hour notification.

## 4. Scope conditions — do not over-apply the 24-hour figure

1. **The TSP derogation is conditional.** It applies only to significant incidents "that have an impact on the provision of its trust services" (Art. 23(4), 2nd subpara.). A trust service provider that is also an essential or important entity and that suffers a significant incident *not* affecting the provision of its trust services falls back on the general regime — 72 hours for the incident notification.
2. **"Significant incident" is a defined trigger, not a judgement call to be deferred.** Under Art. 23(3) an incident is significant if it has caused or is capable of causing severe operational disruption of the services or financial loss for the entity, or has affected or is capable of affecting other natural or legal persons by causing considerable material or non-material damage. The obligation attaches on "reasonable degree of certainty" that such an incident has occurred; waiting for full forensic confirmation burns the clock.
3. **"Without undue delay" is the primary obligation; the hour figure is the outer limit.** Notification must be made as soon as the entity is in a position to do so. Reaching the 24 h / 72 h boundary is compliance with the backstop, not with the obligation.
4. **Recipients of services.** Where the incident is likely to affect the provision of the services concerned, affected recipients must also be informed without undue delay, insofar as they are identifiable (Art. 23(2)); this runs in parallel with, and is not satisfied by, the authority notification.

## 5. Operative procedure for the entity

1. **T0 = awareness.** Record the timestamp at which the entity (not a third party) had a reasonable degree of certainty that a significant incident had occurred. Every deadline below is computed from T0.
2. **T0 + 24 h — early warning** to the CSIRT (or, where the Member State so designates, the competent authority): suspected unlawful/malicious cause, possible cross-border impact.
3. **T0 + 24 h (TSP) or T0 + 72 h (all others) — incident notification:** update of the early warning, initial assessment of severity and impact, indicators of compromise where available.
4. **On request — intermediate report** on status.
5. **Incident notification + 1 month — final report:** detailed description, severity and impact, likely threat type or root cause, applied and ongoing mitigation, cross-border impact where applicable.
6. **If still ongoing at step 5** — progress report at that point, final report within one month of the entity's handling of the incident.
7. Log each submission with timestamp, channel, addressee and content hash; retain as compliance evidence.

## 6. Jurisdictional caveat (material to the answer's use)

The figures above are the **Directive's** harmonised timeframes under Directive (EU) 2022/2555 as adopted. The Directive is transposed into national law, and the applicable deadline for a given entity is the one in the national transposing measure and any regulator guidance, which may shorten or add to the Directive's timeframes and may designate a different recipient than the CSIRT. Belgium, for example, reproduces the 24 h/72 h split (CCB, *NIS2 Notification Guide* v1.3, §B: "within 72 hours (24 hours for trusted service providers) of becoming aware of the significant incident, the entity submits an incident notification"). Before relying on 24 h/72 h operationally, confirm the transposing act of the Member State of establishment/main establishment and any sectoral competent-authority guidance.

## 7. Source verification

- Directive (EU) 2022/2555, Art. 23(3)–(4) — operative text as quoted in §2 (reproduced text of Art. 23).
- Belgian CCB, *NIS2 Notification Guide* v1.3 (Aug 2025), §B and n.3 (citing Art. 35 of the Belgian NIS2 law) — corroborates the 72 h general / 24 h trust-service-provider split.
- Both sources independently state the same pair of figures and the same addressee mapping; no divergence found. No conflicting value was located that would displace 24 h / 72 h at Directive level.
